life of the spirit who remains faithful to the good and the
true; and this we can do whatever the distress and hardship
of the present hour. Anyone may experience the strengthen-
ing power of the spirit who fulfils his duties with such loyalty.
It must not be the self-seeking urge to snatch as much as
possible for oneself, to save one's own skin at all costs, which
determines the course of our daily life, but rather the sway
of honesty and kindness in our hearts even in the face of
cruel hardship. How much easier could men make their
own lot if they met each other in the spirit of friendliness
and good will, were prepared to allow to the other fellow his
due, and to bear with patience the misunderstandings which
are unavoidable! How unnecessarily hard men make life
for themselves by their impatience and bitterness, their
unfriendliness and lovelessness! But whoever remains faithful
to the life of the spirit will always find such as share his faith.
Such faith is the basis of true fellowship; and fellowship in
the life of the spirit sustains and strengthens by its inner
bonds, and is also effectively manifested in outward helpfulness.
V
There is still one final thing to be said. We have asked the
question: can we, in the midst of the distress and hardship
which weighs on our life, still remain anchored in the world
of the spirit and of grace? Paul's answer is: not only are we
able to do so, but it is this very suffering itself which leads us
to depend on the world of grace. Let us note this fact: the
first verses of his paradoxes link the antitheses between this-
worldly realities and the life of the beyond by means of the
conjunction "but":
"We are afflicted in every way but not crushed,
Perplexed but not driven to despair,
Persecuted but not forsaken,
Struck down but not destroyed."
